p: European exploration of the region began in the last three years of the 15th century and continued into the 16th, led by Portuguese explorers after the Cape Route had been found. The Portuguese called the whole region they reached the Indies. Christopher Columbus, who had grossly underestimated the westward distance from Europe to Asia, at first took the New World for the easternmost part of the Indies. To avoid confusion the Americas came to be called the West Indies, also the New Indies or Little Indies, and the original Indies the East Indies, also the Old Indies or Great Indies.

The term has had a broad and a narrow sense. In the Age of Discovery it covered the coasts of the Indian subcontinent and the Indochinese Peninsula together with the Malay Archipelago. In the narrow sense it meant the Malay Archipelago alone, which today comprises the Indonesian Archipelago, New Guinea and the Philippine Archipelago. The former Dutch New Guinea, however, is geographically counted as part of Melanesia and is not included.

Parts of the region are sometimes named after the colonial empire that held them. The Spanish East Indies, the Philippines, were Spanish territory for 333 years before the American conquest and later independence. The Dutch East Indies kept that name for about 300 years until Indonesian independence, and British East Indies refers to Malaysia. The term may also take in the former French Indochina, the former British territories of Brunei, Hong Kong and Singapore, and the former Portuguese Macau and Timor.

The peoples of the region are culturally very diverse and do not consider themselves a single ethnic group. Most are Austronesians, whose ancestors first expanded from the island of Taiwan. In the early modern period Han Chinese began to migrate south and became known as the Peranakans or Straits Chinese. Buddhism, Christianity, Islam and Hinduism are the most widespread religions.

After the founding of European trading companies in the 17th century, among them the British East India Company and the Dutch East India Company, the Indies were important sources of trade goods, particularly cotton, indigo and spices. The name East Indian was once applied to people of all the East Indies, to keep them apart from the indigenous peoples of the Americas, who were then simply called Indians. In colonial times South-East Asians who were not from India were also called Indians. Today the inhabitants of the region are not called East Indians.

notes: The article is short and partly inconsistent (it says the East Indies 'consisted of India' in one place and gives the wider senses elsewhere; it says inhabitants are 'never called East Indians' and also that 'East Indian was once primarily used' for them). I gave both as past and present usage.
The article says the narrow sense includes New Guinea but excludes former Dutch New Guinea; I kept both statements as it gives them.
